prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

You love a woman and you wonder where she goes all night in some tricked- out taxicab, with her high heels and her corset and her big, fat mouth. You love how she only wears her glasses with you, how thick and cow-eyed she swears it’s only ever you she wants to see. You love her, you want her very ugly. If she is lovely big, you want her scrawny. If she is perfect lithe, you want her ballooned, a cosmonaut. How not to love her, her bouillabaisse, her orangina. When you took her to the doctor the doctor said, “Wow, look at that!” and you were proud, you asshole, you love and that’s how you are in love. Any expert, observing human bodies, can see how she’s exceptional, how she ruins us all. But you really love this woman, how come no one can see this? Everyone must become suddenly very clumsy at recognizing beauty if you are to keep her. You don’t want to lose anything, at all, ever. You want her sex depilated, you want everyone else not blind, but perhaps paralyzed, from the eyes down. You wonder where she goes all night. If she leaves you, you will know everything about love. If she’s leaving you now, you already know it.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker is intensely in love with a woman but is tormented by suspicion about where she goes at night.
- The speaker desires the woman possessively, wanting her beauty altered or hidden so others cannot desire her.
- The woman is portrayed as exceptional and physically captivating, even to outsiders like the doctor.
- The speaker’s love is mixed with jealousy, insecurity, and a fear of losing her.
- The possibility of her leaving is presented as something the speaker already senses and equates with fully understanding love.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores possessive, jealous love through a second-person monologue that catalogs the beloved’s body, allure, secrecy, and imagined transformations. It reveals that the speaker’s devotion is inseparable from insecurity and control, suggesting that fear of loss can distort love into a desire to diminish or hide what makes the beloved exceptional.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: You, How, When

outputs.L1:
You love a woman, and you wonder where she goes all night in some tricked-out taxicab, wearing her high heels, her corset, and her big, fat mouth. You love that she wears her glasses only with you—how thick-lensed and cow-eyed she is when she swears it is only ever you she wants to see. You love her; you want her very ugly. If she is lovely and full, you want her scrawny. If she is perfectly lithe, you want her ballooned, a cosmonaut. How could you not love her—her bouillabaisse, her Orangina? When you took her to the doctor, the doctor said, “Wow, look at that!” and you were proud, you asshole; you love, and that is how you are in love.

Any expert observing human bodies can see how exceptional she is, how she ruins us all. But you really love this woman—how is it that no one can see that? Everyone must suddenly become very clumsy at recognizing beauty if you are to keep her. You do not want to lose anything, at all, ever. You want her sex depilated; you want everyone else not blind, exactly, but perhaps paralyzed from the eyes down. You wonder where she goes all night. If she leaves you, you will know everything about love. If she is leaving you now, you already know it.
outputs.L2: You adore a woman, and you lie awake imagining where she disappears to through the night in some flashy cab, wearing heels, a corset, and that loud, enormous mouth of hers. You cherish the fact that she puts on her glasses only when she is with you, those heavy lenses making her eyes look soft and bovine, while she insists that you are the only person she ever wants to look at. You love her so much that you want her made unattractive. If she is beautifully full, you wish her thin and bony. If she is flawlessly slender, you wish her swollen and round, like an astronaut sealed in a suit. How could you fail to love her—her stew of a body, her orange-soda brightness. When you brought her to the physician, he said, “Wow, look at that!” and you felt proud, you jerk; this is what your love looks like, this is how you behave inside it. Anyone trained to examine bodies would recognize that she is extraordinary, that she makes everyone else seem diminished. But you truly love this woman—why is that invisible to everyone? For you to keep her, the whole world would have to become abruptly inept at identifying beauty. You cannot bear to give up even the smallest thing, not now, not ever. You want her body stripped bare of hair; you want other people still able to see, but maybe frozen from the eyes downward. You keep asking yourself where she spends the night. If she walks away from you, you will understand love completely. If she is already walking away, then you understand it already.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents himself as deeply and intensely in love with a woman, but his love is shadowed by anxiety and suspicion. He is not simply admiring her from a distance; he is emotionally consumed by her presence and by the fear that she may be beyond his control. His thoughts return obsessively to the question of where she goes at night, suggesting that his devotion is inseparable from doubt. Love, for him, is not peaceful or secure, but restless and tormenting.

This desire is also strongly possessive. The speaker does not only want the woman to love him; he wants to prevent others from seeing her as desirable. Her beauty becomes a source of suffering because it attracts attention and awakens his jealousy. He imagines wanting that beauty to be changed, hidden, or diminished so that no one else can desire her. In this way, his love becomes controlling: he would rather see her altered than risk sharing her admiration with the world.

The woman herself is portrayed as extraordinary and physically captivating. Her attractiveness is not merely the speaker’s private illusion, but something recognized by others as well. Even an outsider such as the doctor is affected by her appearance, which reinforces the speaker’s sense that she has a power over everyone who sees her. She is shown almost as an irresistible figure, someone whose beauty creates fascination, desire, and unease.

Because of this, the speaker’s love is deeply conflicted. It contains passion and admiration, but also jealousy, insecurity, and fear. He loves the woman intensely, yet that love makes him vulnerable. The more he desires her, the more he fears losing her. His suspicion about her nighttime movements and his wish to conceal her beauty reveal a profound lack of trust and a desperate need for reassurance.

The thought that she might leave him becomes central to his understanding of love. Her departure is not presented as a distant possibility, but as something he already senses approaching. He seems to believe that to love fully is to recognize the danger of loss. In his mind, love is inseparable from the fear that the beloved may disappear, choose someone else, or move beyond his reach. Thus, his experience of love is defined not only by desire, but by the painful awareness that he cannot truly possess the woman he loves.
outputs.L4:
The text presents love as an intense, possessive, and deeply jealous emotion. Framed as a second-person monologue, it addresses the beloved directly, lingering over the details of their body, beauty, and presence. The speaker catalogs the beloved’s physical allure almost obsessively, as if naming each feature could bring it under control. This attention appears affectionate at first, but it gradually reveals a more troubling impulse: the beloved is admired not simply as a person, but as something rare, desirable, and therefore vulnerable to being noticed by others.

Throughout the monologue, the speaker’s devotion is inseparable from insecurity. The beloved’s attractiveness becomes a source of anxiety rather than joy, because it makes them visible to the world. Their secrecy, mystery, and power to transform in the speaker’s imagination intensify this fear. The speaker seems fascinated by what makes the beloved exceptional, yet also threatened by it. Love becomes bound up with suspicion: every sign of beauty or independence suggests the possibility of loss.

As the text develops, the speaker’s jealousy turns into a desire to conceal, reduce, or possess the beloved completely. Rather than celebrating the beloved’s radiance, the speaker imagines ways to hide it from others or diminish its effect. This reveals the darker side of their attachment. The speaker wants to protect the beloved, but that protection begins to resemble control. Their love is not purely generous; it is shaped by fear, envy, and the need to secure what cannot truly be owned.

In this way, the text explores how fear of loss can distort love. The speaker’s passion is real, but it is also unstable, driven by the terror that the beloved’s beauty and freedom might draw them away. What begins as admiration becomes an attempt to contain the very qualities that inspired that admiration in the first place. The monologue ultimately suggests that possessive love is self-contradictory: it claims to adore what is extraordinary, yet it also wishes to diminish or hide that extraordinariness in order to keep it safe.
outputs.L5:
**You, How, and When**

You are the starting point of every change in your life. Before anything can improve, begin, or grow, you must first decide that it matters to you. Your choices, your effort, and your mindset shape the direction you take.

How you move forward is just as important as the decision itself. Progress does not always require a perfect plan, but it does require action. You can learn step by step, ask questions, make mistakes, and improve along the way. The “how” often becomes clearer once you begin.

When should you start? The answer is simple: now. Waiting for the perfect moment can keep you standing still. There may never be a time when everything feels easy or certain. But even a small action today can create momentum for tomorrow.

You decide. You learn how. You begin when you are ready—but the best time is often sooner than you think.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal second-person prose poem about obsessive love, jealousy, and the fear that a beautiful woman is out all night with someone else.
counterfactuals.output:
You imagine her as a white dress moving through the city without touching the ground.

All night the windows keep their little yellow eyes open. All night the streetlamps bend toward one another, whispering. You sit in the room you have made into a shrine and a trap: her photograph pinned above the sink, her hair coiled in a matchbox, the glass she once drank from glowing faintly with the bruise of her mouth. Every object repeats her name until the walls grow damp with it.

You tell yourself she is sleeping. You tell yourself she is alone. But the clock has teeth, and with each hour it chews another hole in your belief.

Somewhere, you think, she is laughing in a room full of smoke. Somewhere a stranger’s hand is learning the geography you worshipped from afar: the cathedral of her throat, the pale avenues of her wrists, the dark orchard of her hair. You see her leaning close to him beneath a chandelier that drips black honey. You see his mouth near her ear, planting little knives there. You see her smile—not the one she gives the world, not the one she gave you once by accident, but the secret one, the warm one, the one you have fed for months in your dreams until it became a starving animal.

Jealousy enters you like a second skeleton.

It stands behind your ribs and wears you. It makes you pace. It makes you press your face to the cold window and search the street for omens: a taxi coughing at the curb, a pair of lovers stitched together under an umbrella, the moon caught in the branches like a torn stocking. Every sound is her return. Every silence is her betrayal.

You become certain she is everywhere except where you need her to be.

In your mind she passes from bar to bar, luminous and cruel, while men turn to ash around her. She drinks red wine and it becomes blood in the glass. She dances, and the floorboards bloom with roses that smell of graves. She throws back her head, and the stars fall into her open mouth. Someone touches her waist. Someone says her name as if it belongs to him.

Your hands close around nothing.

Love, you discover, is not a flower but a room with no doors. You have been living there for so long you have begun to call the darkness furniture. You have arranged your longing carefully: the bed where you do not sleep, the mirror where your face grows thinner, the chair where absence sits with crossed legs, perfumed and patient.

By dawn you are hollowed out, full of birds.

When she finally appears in your imagination—because she does not appear at the door, because the stairs remain mute, because the city refuses to give her back—she is walking beside the river with a man whose face keeps changing into yours. His arm is around her shoulders. Or perhaps it is a shadow. Or perhaps it is the night itself, claiming what you never possessed.

And you understand, with a clarity that feels like frost spreading over glass, that the most terrible rival is not another body.

It is the world.

The world with its lit rooms, its open mouths, its music leaking from basements, its strangers who can stand beside her in line, breathe her air, make her turn her head. The world that receives her whenever she leaves you behind in the kingdom of your closed eyes.

Morning comes pale and indifferent.

You sit among the ruins of your vigil, listening to the first birds rehearse their tiny accusations. The photograph above the sink smiles without mercy. The matchbox is empty. The glass is only glass.

Still, somewhere beneath your skin, jealousy keeps walking.

It wears her perfume.

It knows the way home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary monologue in the voice of a possessive lover who both worships and resents his girlfriend’s beauty, using grotesque imagery and unexpected humor.
counterfactuals.output:
You have no idea what it is like to sit across from you at breakfast.

There you are, buttering toast as if the world has not just rearranged its bones around your face. The kettle screams, the pipes complain, a pigeon on the windowsill looks in and immediately loses the will to continue being a pigeon. And you—my ruin, my cathedral, my little public hazard—ask whether we’re out of marmalade.

Marmalade! While your hair falls over one eye like a velvet curtain in a theater where the play is always my humiliation.

I resent it, you know. I resent your beauty the way a village resents a volcano: with awe, with prayer, with a deep suspicion that one morning I will wake up under ash. You move through rooms and leave dents in the air. Men look at you and become furniture. Women look at you and silently revise their eyebrows. Even dogs behave with a kind of moral confusion, wagging at you as if you are both sausage and sunrise.

And I am expected to be normal about this.

I am expected to say, “Darling, you look lovely,” in the casual tone of a man commenting on a lamp. But you do not look lovely. A lamp looks lovely. A well-iced bun looks lovely. You look like something painted on the inside of a saint’s skull during a fever. You look like God was drunk, lonely, and trying to make an apology to marble.

When you smile, I feel my soul crawl out of my body like a pale grub and offer itself to you on a teaspoon. Disgusting. Undignified. Entirely your fault.

Do not laugh. That’s another crime. Your laugh is intolerable. It has the nerve to be both golden and slightly stupid, like a trumpet falling down stairs. I love it so much I want to put a tiny padlock on your mouth and keep the key under my tongue, which is, I admit, not a healthy image and would make kissing logistically difficult. Still. The impulse exists. I report it as one reports weather: possessive with scattered showers of shame.

Because yes, I want you hidden. There. I’ve said it. I want curtains, veils, a moat, perhaps a tasteful hedge maze with misleading signage. I want to keep you from the eyes of baristas and bus drivers and men in museums who pretend to admire Greek torsos while actually waiting for you to walk past the sculpture and improve on antiquity.

But I also want you seen.

That is the worst of it.

I want the whole city to stop and understand what I have understood: that your face is not a face but an event, a municipal emergency, a gorgeous infestation. I want crowds to gasp and clutch one another. I want philosophers to drop their books into puddles. I want pigeons to organize. I want a commemorative plaque screwed into the pavement wherever you pause to tie your shoe.

And then, the moment they see, I hate them for seeing.

A clean arrangement, isn’t it? Very sane. Very modern. I should have it printed on a mug.

I worship you, but not peacefully. My devotion has elbows. It knocks things over. It eats too quickly. It has a smell, frankly—something between incense, wet wool, and panic. I kneel before you in my mind and immediately complain about the draft. I build altars to your cheekbones and then kick them because other people may visit.

Your beauty makes me petty. Before you, I was almost noble in small quantities. I could admire a sunset without wishing to draw a mustache on it. Now the moon rises and I think, amateur. Flowers bloom and I mutter, try harder. The sea flashes under the sun and I say, yes, but have you seen her collarbone when she reaches for the top shelf?

You have spoiled creation for me. I hope you’re pleased.

And yet I resent you most when you are unaware of it. When you sit there with a smear of jam at the corner of your mouth, reading the back of a cereal box as though you are not personally responsible for half my madness. When you yawn, and your beauty becomes sleepy, slack-jawed, mammalian—oh, the betrayal! Even then, even with your hair in a mutiny and one sock sagging, you remain unbearable. You could sneeze into a napkin and I would want the napkin canonized.

This is not romance. Romance is violins, balconies, moonlight behaving itself. This is more like being haunted by a pastry. A divine pastry, yes. A pastry with opinions. A pastry who steals my side of the blanket and says, “Move over,” as if empires have not collapsed for less.

Sometimes I look at you and feel love so large it becomes almost comic, like trying to store a whale in a teacup. My chest creaks. My ribs look at the situation and submit formal complaints. There is no room in me for how much I adore you, so it leaks out as jealousy, as sarcasm, as the sudden urge to stand too close when someone at a party makes you laugh.

Forgive me. Or don’t. I have no defense.

Only this: that loving you is like being given a priceless vase and then discovering it has legs and wants to go dancing in crowded rooms.

Of course I panic.

Of course I follow with both hands out, useless and anxious, whispering, careful, careful, while you whirl under the lights, bright as a blade, cruel as dessert, beautiful as something I will never deserve and cannot stop reaching for.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a flash fiction piece addressed to “you” about loving a woman so intensely that you want the rest of the world to stop seeing her.
counterfactuals.output:
You love her so much that, some mornings, you resent the sun.

It enters without knocking, lays its gold hands on her face, and there she is—made visible again. The curve of her shoulder above the sheet. The sleep-warm crease beside her mouth. The lashes trembling as if she is dreaming of somewhere you cannot follow.

Outside, the city begins its daily theft.

Windows brighten. Buses sigh at the curb. Somewhere, strangers button their coats and prepare to look at her.

You imagine them: the barista learning her name, the old man on the train noticing the way she reads with one finger pressed to the page, the child in the park staring because she laughs like bells dropped into water. You imagine the world collecting pieces of her without permission, carrying them away in pockets, in glances, in memories they do not deserve.

You hate them for it.

Then she wakes and says, “What?”

You must have made a sound.

“Nothing,” you say.

She squints at you, suspicious and beautiful, and the room expands around her. She is not yours in the way a door is yours, or a cup, or a house you can lock. She is yours only because each day she chooses to return, and even that is a miracle with wings.

Still, when she dresses, you wish for fog. A great white hush rolling down every avenue. You wish for a power outage, for rain thick as curtains, for the whole world to go blind just long enough for her to cross it untouched by anyone’s eyes.

At the door, she kisses you quickly.

“See you tonight,” she says.

And because you love her—not gently, not reasonably, but truly—you let her go.

All day, the world sees her.

All day, it does not end.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental paragraph about romantic insecurity, bodily desire, and paranoia, with vivid strange details like taxis, glasses, doctors, and nighttime disappearances.
counterfactuals.output: At night I became convinced love was a cab with its roof light off, idling just beyond the corner, refusing to take me anywhere. I watched your glasses on the bedside table gather the moon into two cold, clinical lenses, as if they belonged not to you but to some doctor who had examined my longing and found it malignant. When you touched me, my body answered before my mind could file its objections; my skin leaned toward you with the humiliating faith of a dog, while my thoughts crawled under the door and listened for evidence. Every disappearance became anatomical: you stepped out for cigarettes and I felt a rib go missing, you took a taxi home alone and my mouth filled with the taste of rubber and rain, you turned your face away and I saw white coats gathering at the foot of the bed, whispering diagnoses into their sleeves. I wanted you so badly I began to suspect you of being invented by my hunger, a beautiful symptom with wet hair, leaving black fingerprints on the mirror, vanishing before dawn into streets where the traffic lights blinked like sleepless eyes.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a raw, poetic, slightly absurd piece in second person about a man realizing that if the woman he loves leaves him, he will finally understand love.
counterfactuals.output:
You sit at the kitchen table with your hands around a cup of coffee gone cold as a drowned star, and you watch her put on her coat.

Not dramatically. Not like in the movies, where violins crawl out of the wallpaper and everyone’s face becomes a country at war. She is only putting on her coat. One sleeve, then the other. A button. A small cough. Her hair caught under the collar and then freed.

And in that tiny mercy, you feel the universe begin to remove its teeth.

You think: if she leaves, I will understand love.

Not while she stays. No. While she stays, love is groceries, arguments about the window being open, her foot touching yours under the blanket, the wet blue toothbrush beside your own, a pear ripening too fast in the bowl. While she stays, love is a dog asleep in the sun of the ordinary. Love is stupid. Love is a spoon. Love is you saying, do we have onions, and her saying, look.

But if she leaves—

Ah.

If she leaves, the spoon becomes holy.

The toothbrush becomes a relic.

The pear becomes a small yellow planet you failed to inhabit correctly.

You will walk through rooms like a priest of vanished furniture. You will bless the chair where she folded herself, bless the cup her mouth once knew, bless the crack in the ceiling she used to say looked like a running horse, though you never saw it, though you only said yes because you wanted to live in the same weather as her.

If she leaves, the horse will appear.

Galloping. Ridiculous. Late.

You have been a man, which is to say a locked box trying to sing. You have loved her with the blunt instruments given to you: bread, silence, your body, rent money, a hand on her back in crowded places. You have loved her like a man carrying a glass of water through a burning house, proud he has not spilled it, blind to the fact that she is the fire.

She says your name.

You hate how human it sounds in her mouth.

You want to drop to your knees, but your knees are old governments and do not negotiate with the heart. So you sit there, stupidly alive. The coffee cools. The refrigerator hums its single-note opera. Somewhere, a neighbor laughs, murdering you casually through the wall.

You realize you have never understood love because you have always had somewhere to put it.

Into her hands.
Into her hair.
Into the envelope of her sleep.
Into the warm animal of her being beside you in bed.

But if she leaves, love will have no address.

It will wander in you, knocking on ribs, licking the windows, wearing her dress and your father’s boots. It will sit in the bathtub and smoke. It will eat all the salt. It will call you darling in the voice of a crow.

Then you will know it.

Then, finally, when there is no her to receive it, no her to correct your terrible posture, no her to say you’re burning the garlic, no her to turn toward you in the night as if your body were still a place worth returning to—

then love will stand in the doorway.

Naked.

Unemployed.

Holding a fish.

And it will say: now do you see me?

And you will.

God help you, you will.

You will see that love was never the staying, never the leaving, never the soft machinery of two people making a life out of laundry and weather reports. Love was the panic under all of it. The animal trembling beneath the floorboards. The impossible wish to be known and not destroyed. The old, bright wound saying, take me with you, take me with you, even into the next room.

She picks up her bag.

It is not a large bag.

This offends you. That the end of the world should fit into something with a zipper.

You want to tell her: wait. I am about to become wise. I am about to become a cathedral of regret. I am about to understand everything, and it will be useless, and I would rather be an idiot with you.

But your mouth is a ruined mailbox. Nothing gets delivered.

So you watch her reach for the door.

And for one clean second, before she opens it, you love her perfectly.

Not as possession. Not as hunger. Not as the mirror where you check that you still exist.

You love her as departure.

As weather.

As a bird refusing the hand.

As the knife that teaches the apple its own sweetness.

And you understand, almost.

Almost.

Then the door opens, and the hallway light pours in like milk from a broken moon.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
